definition: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and without any clear reason.
example: Sailors distrusted the capricious winds near the cape, which could shift direction in minutes.
nuance: Capricious stresses impulsive whim behind the changes, while erratic can describe any irregular pattern, even a machine's.
prompt: Employees describe how their manager sets the rules in their office.
options: The capricious manager banned headphones on Monday, then required them on Friday for no stated reason.
The capricious manager's corner office was roomy enough to hold thirty desks with space to spare.
The capricious manager kept the same clear rules in place for ten years, and everyone knew them.
The capricious manager changed one policy only after a month of surveys and a detailed memo.
reasons: Abrupt reversals with no explanation behind them are exactly the kind of whim the word names.
Spaciousness belongs to the look-alike capacious; this word concerns unpredictable whims.
Rules that stay fixed for a decade show steadiness, the reverse of impulsive change.
A slow, carefully documented decision is deliberate, not a sudden whim.

practice.prompt: A family explains how their cat behaves around visitors.
options: Our capricious cat curls up on a guest's lap, then hisses and stalks off for no clear reason.
Our capricious cat learned to open the pantry door when she was only ten weeks old.
Our capricious cat greets every visitor with the same slow blink and gentle purr, without fail.
Our capricious cat is so dependably sweet that we recommend her to anyone nervous around pets.
reasons: Affection that flips to hostility without cause fits the word's sense of unpredictable mood.
Skill at a young age suggests precocious, a different word; nothing here shows shifting moods.
Behaving identically every time is consistency, the opposite of whimsical shifts.
Calling a pet dependable contradicts the word, which signals moods no one can count on.
